title: The Genealogy and Birth of Jesus the Messiah
summary: Matthew opens with the family line of Jesus, traced from Abraham through King David and the exile to Joseph, arranged in three sets of fourteen generations and including four women from Israel's past. Then he tells how Mary, engaged to Joseph, was found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit. An angel tells Joseph in a dream to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins, fulfilling Isaiah's promise of Immanuel, God with us.
story: The Old Testament closed with Israel home from exile but still waiting: no king on David's throne, foreign empires in charge, and Malachi's promise of a coming messenger unanswered. Matthew's first line picks up the whole story at once. By calling Jesus the son of David and the son of Abraham, he ties him to the two great promises of the Old Testament, the covenant with Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18) and the covenant with David that his throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). The genealogy retells Israel's history in names, rising to David, falling into the exile, and waiting through obscurity until the Messiah. The birth account then shows that this son of David comes into the line in an unexpected way: by adoption through Joseph and by the power of the Holy Spirit.
historical:
The events are set in the last years of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea for Rome until his death in 4 BC (see chapter 2), so Jesus was probably born a few years before that date. The later calendar that counts years from Jesus' birth, worked out by the monk Dionysius Exiguus in the sixth century AD, missed by several years. Luke's Gospel places Joseph and Mary in Nazareth, a small village in Galilee, before the birth; Matthew first mentions Nazareth when the family settles there after returning from Egypt (2:23).

Genealogies mattered in Second Temple Judaism. Priests had to prove their descent to serve (Ezra 2:61-63), and families of David's line were remembered. Matthew's genealogy differs from Luke's (Luke 3:23-38), which runs backward from Jesus to Adam and follows David's son Nathan rather than Solomon. Interpreters have offered several explanations: that Luke traces Mary's line and Matthew Joseph's; that Matthew gives the royal line of succession and Luke the biological descent; or that levirate marriage (a man marrying his dead brother's widow to raise children in the brother's name, Deuteronomy 25:5-6) produced two legal fathers in one generation, a suggestion already made by Julius Africanus in the third century. None of these is certain, and each has able defenders.
cultural:
A Jewish marriage came in two stages. First came betrothal, a binding agreement made before witnesses, after which the couple were legally husband and wife and could be separated only by divorce, though they did not yet live together. Later came the wedding itself, when the husband took the bride into his home. Mary was pregnant between the two stages. Under the law of Moses, an engaged woman who had been unfaithful could be put to death (Deuteronomy 22:23-24), though in Roman-ruled Judea such penalties were rarely if ever carried out, and the usual outcome was divorce and public shame. Joseph, a righteous man, decides to divorce her quietly, which shows both respect for the law and mercy toward Mary.

Genealogies in the ancient world were not only records of descent. They made claims about status, inheritance, and identity, and they often skipped generations. Matthew's inclusion of women was unusual. Tamar was likely a Canaanite who bore twins to her father-in-law Judah (Genesis 38), Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho (Joshua 2), Ruth was a Moabite (Ruth 1), and Uriah's wife, Bathsheba, was taken by David in adultery (2 Samuel 11). Readers have noticed that each was a Gentile or associated with a Gentile, and each was involved in an irregular or scandalous union, and they have suggested that Matthew includes them to anticipate both the Gentiles' welcome into God's people and the surprising circumstances of Mary's pregnancy.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 17 are a genealogy arranged in three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile, and from the exile to the Messiah. The arrangement is deliberate, as verse 17 says. To make it work, Matthew omits some names, including three kings between Joram and Uzziah (Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah), a common practice in ancient genealogies. Many interpreters suggest the number fourteen was chosen because the Hebrew letters of David's name add up to fourteen (in Hebrew, letters also served as numbers), which would make the whole list a subtle signature of the Davidic king. The pattern A was the father of B breaks at verse 16, where Joseph is called the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, preparing for the story that follows. Verses 18 to 25 are a narrative built around a dream and the first of Matthew's fulfillment formulas (verse 22), which will recur throughout the Gospel.

outline.t: Title: Jesus the Messiah, son of David, son of Abraham
From the exile to the Messiah
Mary is found with child; Joseph's decision
The angel's message and the Immanuel prophecy
Joseph obeys and names the child Jesus

doctrines.note: Jesus is presented at once as the Christ, the anointed king, legally the son of David through Joseph's adoption and heir of the promises to Abraham. The genealogy shows that Israel's history has been moving toward him.

The conception of Jesus is the work of the Holy Spirit, and the child is called Immanuel, God with us. From its first chapter Matthew speaks of God, the Spirit, and the Son together, a pattern that culminates in the one name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in 28:19.
The name Jesus means the LORD saves, and the angel explains the name: he will save his people from their sins. Matthew defines the Messiah's rescue first as rescue from sin, not only from Rome.

words.note: Genesis, origin, birth, or lineage. It appears in verse 1 (the record of the genealogy, literally the book of the genesis) and verse 18 (the birth). The same phrase appears in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, and many readers think Matthew is signaling that a new beginning has come.

Parthenos, virgin. In Greek the word normally means a young woman who has not had sexual relations. Isaiah 7:14 in Hebrew uses almah, a young woman of marriageable age, but the Greek translation of Isaiah, made by Jews in the second century BC or so, used parthenos, and Matthew quotes that text. Matthew's narrative makes his meaning explicit in verses 18 and 25.

Sozo, to save, rescue, or heal. In the Gospels it covers rescue from danger, healing from disease, and deliverance from sin and judgment. The angel ties it to the name Jesus (Greek Iesous, from the Hebrew Yeshua or Joshua, meaning the LORD saves).

Emmanouel, Immanuel, from Hebrew words meaning God with us, as Matthew translates. The name frames the whole Gospel: it opens here and is echoed in the last verse, where the risen Jesus promises to be with his disciples always (28:20).

christ: Matthew's first chapter answers the question who Jesus is with three claims. He is the son of David, the rightful king of Israel. He is the son of Abraham, the one through whom the nations will be blessed. And he is Immanuel, God with us, conceived by the Holy Spirit. The fulfillment formula of verse 22 introduces Isaiah 7:14: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”). The church has confessed from its earliest creeds that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, and has seen in this the mystery of one person who is truly God and truly human. The genealogy's inclusion of Gentiles and sinners, and its passage through the disaster of the exile, also shows the kind of Savior he is: one who enters a real family history, with its failures, in order to save his people from their sins.

hard.q: Did Isaiah 7:14 really predict a virgin birth, and what does verse 25 imply about Mary afterward?
hard.a:
In its own context Isaiah 7:14 was given to King Ahaz around 735 BC, during a war with Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel, as a sign that before a child born soon would grow up, those enemies would be gone. The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age and does not by itself specify virginity. Some interpreters therefore read Isaiah as having an immediate fulfillment in his own day and a fuller one in Jesus, a pattern Matthew uses elsewhere. Others argue that the sign, especially in light of Isaiah 9:6-7, pointed beyond Ahaz's time to a unique child all along. Either way, Matthew follows the Greek translation made by Jews before the Christian era, which already used the word for virgin, and the virgin conception is confessed by the church on the basis of Matthew and Luke's accounts, not on Isaiah alone.

Verse 25 says Joseph had no union with Mary until she gave birth. Protestants usually read this, together with the mention of Jesus' brothers and sisters (13:55-56), to mean that Mary and Joseph later had other children. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding to Mary's perpetual virginity, note that until in Greek need not imply a change afterward and understand the brothers as cousins or as Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. This is a second-order question on which Christians differ.

questions: The genealogy includes kings and nobodies, heroes and scandals. What does it suggest about the kind of family history God is willing to work through, including yours?
Joseph had to choose between protecting his reputation and obeying a message that made no sense to his neighbors. When has obedience cost you in the eyes of others?
Matthew says the name Jesus means he will save his people from their sins. What do people today most want to be saved from, and how does that compare?
